justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook anchored around current price or index levels, with only modest drift upward across the three horizons. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 47.15 is essentially a mean-reversion assumption — absent a major catalyst, most assets or indicators tend to close near where they opened, with slight regression toward a short-term moving average. The one-week estimate of 47.30 adds a small positive drift consistent with whatever underlying trend was present at the time of forecasting, while the one-month estimate of 47.50 extends that trend modestly further, reflecting the assumption that gradual upward momentum or fundamental support would persist without a major reversal.

The confidence interval widths widen appropriately as the horizon extends, reflecting the compounding uncertainty over time. At one day, the 90% interval of 45.80 to 48.50 is relatively tight, capturing typical intraday-to-next-day volatility. At one week, the interval widens to 44.50–50.10, incorporating the possibility of several adverse or favorable sessions accumulating. By one month, the interval of 42.50–52.50 spans roughly ten points on either side of the point estimate, which reflects the realistic range of outcomes when macroeconomic data releases, central bank communications, earnings announcements, and shifting sentiment are all given room to play out.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these stated intervals include sudden geopolitical shocks, unexpected central bank policy shifts, or a liquidity event in financial markets — any of which could produce sharp moves well beyond the stated bounds within hours. On the upside, a surprise positive catalyst such as a major policy announcement, blowout economic data, or a short-squeeze dynamic could similarly breach the upper bound of the one-month interval. The stated 90% confidence interval, by construction, leaves a 10% probability mass in the tails, and fat-tail events in financial markets are historically more common than standard distributional assumptions would suggest, meaning real-world breaches may occur more frequently than the stated confidence level implies.
